content: In recent years, bedaquiline has been successfully donated, and delamanid has been made available at reduced costs for low-income countries. Subsequent studies have shown that the risk of dysglycemia is significantly lower in tuberculosis (TB) patients, and the benefits of using gatifloxacin for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) likely outweigh the risks. Clofazimine supplies are also limited, and while it is primarily indicated for leprosy, it is used off-label for MDR-TB treatment. Neither clofazimine nor gatifloxacin is currently included in the World Health Organization (WHO) Model List of Essential Medicines for TB. The programmatic management of drug-resistant TB has become a critical component of many national TB programs. The 2016 WHO guidelines for drug-resistant TB recommend individualized treatment regimens for adults and children with rifampicin-resistant TB or MDR-TB when shorter MDR-TB regimens are not feasible. These regimens should include at least five effective TB medicines during the intensive phase, comprising pyrazinamide and four core second-line TB drugs, with one from Group A, one from Group B, and at least two from Group C. If these minimum requirements cannot be met, agents from Group D2 and Group D3 may be added to reach a total of five effective drugs. Group A drugs include levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and gatifloxacin, with a preference for high-dose levofloxacin, followed by moxifloxacin and gatifloxacin. Ofloxacin should be phased out, and ciprofloxacin should not be used due to limited evidence of effectiveness. Fluoroquinolones are considered essential components of MDR-TB regimens, as they significantly improve treatment outcomes. However, moxifloxacin carries a risk of QT prolongation, particularly when combined with other QT-prolonging drugs like bedaquiline or delamanid. Levofloxacin and gatifloxacin have fewer cardiotoxicity concerns, making them preferable in certain cases. Second-line injectable agents, such as amikacin, capreomycin, and kanamycin, are recommended for adults with rifampicin-resistant TB or MDR-TB unless contraindicated. In children with mild disease, the risks of these agents, including hearing loss and nephrotoxicity, may outweigh the benefits, and their use can be excluded. Streptomycin may be used as an alternative injectable agent if other options are unavailable and the strain is likely susceptible. Adverse effects of second-line injectables, such as hearing loss, nephrotoxicity, and hypersensitivity, should be closely monitored, especially in children, where hearing loss can significantly impact quality of life. Other core second-line agents include ethionamide (or prothionamide), cycloserine (or terizidone), linezolid, and clofazimine. Ethionamide and prothionamide can cause gastrointestinal disturbances and hypothyroidism, which are reversible upon drug cessation. Cycloserine is associated with neuropsychiatric adverse effects, while linezolid can cause severe hematologic toxicities, such as anemia and thrombocytopenia, as well as peripheral and optic neuropathy. Linezolid use requires close monitoring for adverse effects and is best reserved for patients with additional drug resistance or intolerance to other core regimen components. Clofazimine may contribute to the sterilizing function of MDR-TB regimens, particularly when pyrazinamide is ineffective. However, evidence for its efficacy in MDR-TB is primarily based on observational studies, and its use may cause skin discoloration, which can be distressing for patients. Clofazimine should be used cautiously in combination with other QT-prolonging drugs. Add-on agents, such as pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and high-dose isoniazid, are typically included in MDR-TB regimens unless contraindicated. Pyrazinamide is often added by default, although resistance to this drug is common in rifampicin-resistant TB strains. High-dose isoniazid is recommended for strains with low-level resistance, as it can still provide benefit. Ethambutol has limited CNS penetration and should not be relied upon for treating TB meningitis. Group D2 agents, bedaquiline and delamanid, are newer drugs that may be added to MDR-TB regimens in specific cases. WHO interim policies guide their use in adults, but recommendations for children are still under review. Group D3 agents, including para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS), carbapenems (imipenem-cilastatin or meropenem), and clavulanate, are reserved for situations where other options are unavailable. PAS is associated with gastrointestinal disturbances and hypothyroidism, while carbapenems must be used with clavulanate to enhance their efficacy against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. For patients with additional resistance to fluoroquinolones or second-line injectables, or those with extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB), regimens should be adjusted by adding agents from Groups D2 and D3. Rapid diagnostic testing, such as the GenoType MTBDRsl assay, can help identify resistance to fluoroquinolones and injectables, guiding regimen modifications. For TB meningitis caused by rifampicin-resistant or MDR strains, treatment should include drugs with good CNS penetration, such as fluoroquinolones, ethionamide, cycloserine, linezolid, and high-dose isoniazid. Pyrazinamide may also be included, but caution is needed due to potential resistance. Drugs with poor CNS penetration, such as PAS and ethambutol, should not be counted among the effective agents for treating MDR-TB meningitis.
